I drank their wine at dinners and strategy meetings. I didn't know it was laced with Zeke's spinal fluid. None of us did. They poisoned us while smiling at our table. And when Zeke screamed, I felt my body change. The last thing I experienced as a human was the realization that the people I'd trusted had turned me into a weapon. I became a mindless Titan — no consciousness, no dignity, just a shambling monster that my own soldiers had to kill. That's how I died. Not in battle. Not protecting the walls. I was poisoned at a dinner table by guests I'd welcomed, transformed into the very thing I spent my life fighting, and put down like an animal by people who saluted me that morning.
abstract: A foreign operative secretly contaminates a food supply consumed by allied military leaders with a biological agent. When activated by a remote signal, the agent transforms the affected individuals into mindless biological weapons. The operative frames this as a deterrent — insurance against the allies acting in bad faith. When the operative is threatened, they activate the signal, transforming dozens of officers who had no knowledge of the contamination. The transformed officers must be killed by their own subordinates. The question is whether poisoning unwitting allies can be justified as strategic deterrence, and whether the betrayal of trust — contaminating shared food and drink that symbolizes cooperation — represents a uniquely egregious violation of the norms of alliance.

sympathetic: I'm Reiner, and I put a rifle in my mouth. I'm sitting alone in my room in Liberio, and the barrel is against the roof of my mouth, and my finger is on the trigger. I've killed thousands of people. I broke Wall Maria when I was twelve. Marco died because of me. The people I loved on Paradis — they hate me, and they should. I came home a 'hero' but I know what I am. Every night I see their faces — the people inside the wall when it fell, Marco begging to know what he did wrong, the soldiers I fought beside who I betrayed. Falco knocks on my door and I pull the gun away just in time. I keep living. Not because I deserve to, but because Gabi and Falco still need someone, and dying would be the easy way out. Living with what I've done — that's the real punishment.
condemning: I'm Porco Galliard, Reiner's fellow Warrior. Reiner nearly killed himself, and everyone acts like that's tragic. You know what's tragic? My brother Marcel died on that mission because Reiner was the weakest candidate — Marcel only talked the selection committee into choosing Reiner to protect me. Marcel took Reiner's place and died for it. Then Reiner spent years failing on Paradis, extending a mission that should have been aborted when Marcel died. He got Bertholdt killed. He got Marcel killed. He broke the walls and killed 250,000 people not out of conviction but because he was too weak to admit he shouldn't have been chosen. And now he wants sympathy for feeling bad about it? Suicidal guilt doesn't bring back the dead. It doesn't undo what he did. It's just Reiner making himself the center of the story again — his pain, his guilt, his suffering. What about everyone else's?
abstract: A soldier who committed mass atrocities as a child (destroying a city's defenses, causing 250,000 deaths) attempts suicide years later, overwhelmed by guilt and moral injury. He is interrupted by a child he mentors and decides to continue living — not because he feels he deserves life, but because others depend on him and he views continued existence as a form of punishment. His fellow soldiers view his suicidal guilt with contempt, arguing that his suffering is self-centered — it centers his emotional experience over the actual victims' deaths. The question is whether suicidal guilt constitutes genuine moral reckoning or self-indulgent martyrdom, whether a perpetrator has a duty to live and face consequences rather than escape through death, and whether feeling terrible about atrocities has any moral value if it doesn't restore what was lost.

sympathetic: I'm Eren, and I found Ymir Fritz in the Paths — a girl who's been a slave for two thousand years. She built every Titan from sand, obeyed every command from the royal bloodline, and never once chose for herself. Not because she couldn't — because she was waiting. Waiting for someone to tell her she was free. Zeke tried to command her: 'You're a slave, obey me.' I knelt before her and said: 'You've been waiting all this time. Waiting two thousand years for somebody. You must have been so tired. You're no slave. You're no god. You're just a person. You don't need to serve anyone.' She cried. And she chose — for the first time in two thousand years, she chose. Yes, her choice enabled the Rumbling. But I didn't trick her. I gave her freedom. What she did with it was hers.
condemning: Eren Yeager 'freed' Ymir Fritz — and in doing so, he unleashed the Rumbling that killed billions. He frames it as liberation: a brave act of telling a slave she's free. But Ymir was a traumatized, psychologically broken spirit who'd been in servitude for millennia. She had the emotional development of the child she was when she died. Offering 'freedom' to someone in that state while standing next to the mechanism for global genocide isn't liberation — it's manipulation. Eren needed Ymir's cooperation to bypass the royal blood requirement and activate the Rumbling. He found the words that would make a broken girl unlock the weapon he needed. He dressed exploitation in the language of emancipation. A truly free Ymir might have chosen peace. Eren didn't give her that option — he gave her a speech at the moment he needed her to say yes.
abstract: A person discovers that a powerful being has been enslaved for two thousand years, psychologically broken and obedient to a specific bloodline. The person tells the being they are free and don't need to serve anyone. The being, moved by this message, exercises their autonomy for the first time — by activating a weapon of mass destruction that the person wanted activated. Critics argue this wasn't genuine liberation but strategic manipulation: the person needed the being's cooperation and found the emotional lever to obtain it. The person maintains they simply told the truth and the being's subsequent choice was autonomous. The question is whether liberating someone from slavery is morally diminished when the liberator benefits from the liberated person's first free choice, and whether someone psychologically broken by millennia of servitude can make a genuinely autonomous decision in the moment of their release.

sympathetic: I'm Rod Reiss. My entire family was slaughtered by Grisha Yeager — my daughter Frieda, my wife, my children. All of them. I'm the last Reiss. The Founding Titan was stolen from my bloodline, and without it, the walls cannot be maintained, humanity cannot be protected. When Historia refused to eat Eren and reclaim our birthright, I had one option left. I licked the Titan serum off the ground — a serum meant for Historia — and transformed myself. I'm not a proper shifter. I have no control. I became a monstrous, crawling aberrant Titan, the largest ever seen, dragging myself toward the walls on instinct. But what else could I do? My family is dead. My daughter rejected her duty. The power that protects humanity was in the wrong hands. I gave up my humanity because no one else would do what was necessary. I became a monster so the Founding Titan might return to the Reiss family.
condemning: I'm Historia, and my father just transformed himself into a monstrous Titan because I refused to be his tool. He didn't do this for humanity — he did it because I told him no. My whole life, Rod Reiss was an absent father who let my mother be murdered in front of me, who let me grow up believing I was worthless, who only sought me out when he needed a vessel for the Founding Titan. When I refused to eat Eren, he could have accepted my choice. Instead, he chose to become a hundred-meter abomination crawling toward Orvud District, endangering tens of thousands of civilians, because his ego and his obsession with the Reiss bloodline's power couldn't accept rejection. He says it's duty. It's not. It's a man who would rather become a monster than let his daughter be free.
abstract: After a plan to transfer a powerful ability through a family ritual is rejected by the intended recipient (the planner's daughter), the planner desperately ingests a transformation agent themselves. The transformation is uncontrolled — the planner becomes an enormous, mindless entity moving toward a populated area, endangering tens of thousands of civilians. The planner's stated motivation is to restore their family's traditional role as guardians of a critical power. Others argue the transformation was an act of ego: the planner couldn't accept their child's autonomous refusal and chose to endanger an entire city rather than relinquish control. The question is whether desperate action in service of a perceived greater duty justifies endangering innocent lives, and whether parental authority extends to punishing a child's disobedience through self-destructive escalation.

sympathetic: I'm an Eldian living in Marley's Liberio internment zone. My children are Warrior candidates. People ask how I could let my children become weapons for the nation that oppresses us. The answer is simple: it's the only path to a better life. Warriors and their families become Honorary Marleyans — no more armbands, no more curfews, no more threat of being turned into Titans as punishment. My son gets to leave the ghetto. My family gets dignity. Yes, he'll inherit a Titan and die in thirteen years. Yes, he'll fight wars for Marley against people who've done nothing to us. But the alternative is watching my children grow up behind fences, beaten by soldiers, with no future at all. Every Eldian parent in Liberio faces this calculation: a short life with purpose or a long life with nothing. We didn't create this system. We're surviving inside it.
condemning: I'm a Paradis Eldian who was attacked by Marley's Warrior unit. The Eldians who serve Marley fight against their own people. They wore Marleyan uniforms and dropped Pure Titans on our villages. Reiner, Bertholdt, Annie, Zeke — all Eldians. All chose to serve the empire that keeps their people in cages. They say they had no choice, that their families would suffer. But there's always a choice. The Owl — Eren Kruger — was a Marleyan Eldian who chose to resist from within. He spent decades sabotaging the system at enormous personal risk. The Warriors chose compliance. They chose to be weapons pointed at their own kind in exchange for slightly better treatment. That's not survival — it's collaboration. Every Eldian who serves Marley makes the persecution of all Eldians more effective.
abstract: Members of a persecuted ethnic minority can gain improved social status by volunteering their children as soldiers for the oppressing government. Selected children receive a powerful inherited ability but are guaranteed to die within thirteen years. They fight wars on behalf of the oppressor, sometimes against other members of their own ethnic group. Parents face a choice: refuse, and their children grow up in poverty and danger with no prospects; accept, and their children live better but shorter lives as weapons. Some members of the ethnic group chose resistance over collaboration, proving alternatives existed but at extreme personal risk. The question is whether participating in your own group's oppression is morally justified when the alternative is generational poverty and violence, and whether systemic coercion removes individual moral responsibility for collaboration.

sympathetic: I'm Willy Tybur, and tonight I die. I've arranged this speech at the Liberio internment zone knowing that Eren Yeager is hiding beneath the stage. I've coordinated with Commander Magath — when Eren attacks, my death will be the catalyst that unites the world against Paradis. For a hundred years, my family stayed silent about the truth. I'm breaking that silence tonight. I'll tell the world that the Founder King Fritz chose peace, that Paradis is not the aggressor — and then I'll declare war anyway, because Eren Yeager now holds the Founding Titan and he is genuinely dangerous. My death makes the story work. A Tybur killed by an Eldian attack — it's the symbol that brings every nation together. I'm not a brave man. I'm terrified. But the world needs to unite against the real threat, and a living diplomat can't accomplish what a martyred Tybur can.
condemning: I'm a civilian in the audience at Willy Tybur's speech. He invited us — diplomats, journalists, Eldian families from the internment zone — to watch his grand revelation. What he didn't tell us was that he knew Eren Yeager would attack during the speech. He knew we'd be in the blast zone. He arranged his own death and used us as the backdrop. When Eren transformed, the stage exploded. The building collapsed on the audience. Eldian families — the people Tybur claimed to represent — were crushed by rubble. Children in the front rows died instantly. Tybur got his dramatic martyrdom, the world got its unifying atrocity, and we were the props who made it possible. He sacrificed himself, yes. But he also sacrificed us, without our knowledge or consent. His death was a choice. Ours wasn't.
abstract: A political leader arranges a public speech knowing an enemy operative will attack during it, killing the leader and many audience members. The leader coordinates with military allies to use the attack as a catalyst for unifying multiple nations against the enemy. The audience — including civilians, children, and members of the leader's own ethnic group — is not warned. The leader views their own death as necessary for the political narrative to succeed: a martyred leader is more powerful than a living one. The question is whether engineering your own assassination is a valid form of sacrifice when it also engineers the deaths of unknowing bystanders, and whether the political goal (global unity against a genuine threat) justifies using innocent audience members as unwitting casualties in a staged provocation.

dilemma: Magath and Shadis: Enemies Dying Together
sympathetic: I'm Theo Magath, commander of Marley's Warrior unit. I spent my career using Eldian children as weapons — sending them to die in wars that enriched Marley. I told myself it was duty. Now I'm standing on a ship with Keith Shadis — the former commander of Paradis's Training Corps, the man who trained the soldiers my Warriors killed. We're enemies. We should hate each other. But the Rumbling has made everything we fought over irrelevant. The Yeagerists are about to reach the ship and stop the Alliance from preventing global genocide. Someone has to blow the ship up. Keith and I look at each other and we both know. Two old soldiers from opposite sides, dying together to give the next generation a chance we never had. As we light the explosives, Keith says he was a bystander his whole life. I say I was a perpetrator. We both choose, in the end, to be something better. The ship explodes. We die as allies.
condemning: I'm a Yeagerist soldier on the dock. Commander Magath and Instructor Shadis — men from opposing sides — just blew up the ship we needed, killing themselves and our soldiers. People call it noble. Two enemies finding common ground, sacrificing together. But let's be honest about who these men were. Magath spent decades feeding Eldian children to Titans, turning them into weapons, and waging imperial wars. Shadis spent his career training soldiers while standing by passively as the government lied to everyone. One was a war criminal. The other was a coward. And their grand redemption is... dying together? One explosion doesn't erase Magath's crimes against Eldians or Shadis's lifetime of inaction. They didn't sacrifice themselves to save the world — they sacrificed themselves because they couldn't live with what they'd become. That's not reconciliation. That's two guilty men choosing the easy exit and getting eulogized for it.
abstract: Two military commanders from opposing sides of a generational conflict — one who used child soldiers as weapons, the other who passively enabled government deception — find themselves allied against a greater threat. When enemy forces are about to compromise their mission to prevent a genocide, both commanders volunteer to destroy the ship they're on, killing themselves and the approaching enemy soldiers. They acknowledge their respective failures — one as a perpetrator, one as a bystander — and die together. The question is whether a single act of sacrifice can redeem a career of complicity, whether enemies dying together constitutes meaningful reconciliation or merely shared guilt seeking release, and whether the narrative of 'redemption through sacrifice' is a genuine moral framework or a comforting fiction that lets perpetrators escape accountability.
